We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the numbers were presented didn't quite add up for me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy in the item list, specifically how the price for the Wireless Mouse is significantly larger and bolder than the Ergonomic Chair, making it look like the main total rather than an individual item cost.
B) The mathematical inconsistency where the Subtotal ($288.99) matches the Total ($288.99), despite the individual items listed above summing to a much higher amount ($249.00 + $39.99).
C) The placement of the "Total" label at the bottom of the list, which felt buried among the line items rather than standing out clearly as the final figure.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably A? The sizes not forming a clear hierarchy, or not being able to spot the total without reading through everything. I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it.

turns.q: What specific visual cues in that price label make it stand out so much more than the chair's price?
turns.a: I suppose... looking at the price section, I wasn't quite sure which number was the most important one. There were several different sizes of text in that section and I couldn't immediately read the hierarchy from them. Not a dramatic problem — I did find the total after reading through — but it took longer than it should have, I think.

turns.q: What specifically about those varying text sizes makes it difficult for you to distinguish which price belongs to which item?
turns.a: I suppose it was the sizing. There were several different text sizes in that section — some larger, some smaller — but not arranged in any pattern I could follow. So my eye didn't know where to go first. I'm not sure if that was intentional — maybe they wanted to show different levels of detail — but it meant I couldn't scan the section the way I'd normally scan prices.

turns.q: What specific visual arrangement of those mixed sizes makes it impossible for you to group them into a logical pattern?
turns.a: I keep coming back to the same answer — the sizes didn't feel organized in a readable way. I'm not sure I can explain it beyond that. It's one of those things that's easier to feel than to articulate.

turns.q: What would those text sizes need to look like for the list to feel organized and readable?

turns.a: I'm not sure I can describe it differently than I already have. The type sizes didn't form a clear pattern — that's really the whole of it.

turns.a: I think we're going in circles a bit — it comes back to the same thing each time. No clear order, nothing that looked obviously like the total.

turns.a: I'm not entirely sure. Maybe because the numbers were all different sizes but not in a way that felt intentional. I've seen other apps where the total is obviously the main number — you can see it without reading. Here I couldn't do that. I had to read the labels. I don't know if that's a problem or just how this particular layout works.

turns.q: What specific visual treatment would make it immediately obvious which number is the total versus an individual item price?
turns.a: I think it's a structural issue, not a preference. Typographic scales exist precisely for this reason — to communicate hierarchy through size relationships. Having five arbitrary sizes in one small section isn't a style choice, it's a hierarchy that doesn't resolve. Accessibility guidelines speak to minimum readable sizes too, but even beyond that, it's just a question of whether the section is legible at a glance. This one isn't.

turns.q: If you were adjusting that list, what specific change to the text size or style would make the individual item prices look distinct from a total?

turns.q: Would standardizing all item prices to the same smaller size help establish that order, or is it more about adding a distinct label like "Total" to the largest number? Or is there another specific visual cue missing that would make the hierarchy obvious?
turns.a: I'm aware I keep saying the same thing, but it really does come down to that — there were too many different sizes and none of them clearly meant "this is the most important." I don't have a sharper way to phrase it.
